title: Servers, routing and MVC
subtitle: What happens on the other side of the request: routing, business logic, the database and the response.

req.title: Request → response
req.body: A server listens on a port, parses the request, routes it to a handler, does the work (read/write a database, call services), and builds a response. A minimal Node handler: app.get('/hello', (req, res) => res.send('hi')).

mid.title: Middleware
mid.body: Middleware are functions that see every request in order: logging, parsing JSON, authentication, then the route handler; each may respond or call next(). Order matters: authentication must run before the handler it protects.

mvc.title: MVC
mvc.body: Model: data and business rules; View: templates that render HTML; Controller: maps requests to model calls and picks a view. The router hands a request to the controller, which asks the model, then renders a view.

db.title: Databases from code
db.body: Use parameterised queries — never build SQL by pasting user input. An ORM maps tables to classes. Cache hot reads (Redis) and index the columns you filter by.
db.steps: A product lookup takes 20 ms from the database, 1 ms from cache. 90 % of reads hit the cache. Average = 0.9·1 + 0.1·20.

sess.title: State: cookies and sessions
sess.body: HTTP is stateless, so after login the server issues a session id in a cookie; the browser sends it with every request and the server looks up the session. Cookies should be HttpOnly (not readable by JS), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite.

scale.title: Scaling a server
scale.body: Add servers behind a load balancer; keep servers stateless (sessions in a shared store) so any can answer. Put static files on a CDN. If one server handles 200 requests/s, how many for 1500 req/s with 25 % headroom?
